## 3.1 Device and network abuse

Applies to the app and to any SDK it includes. Foreground services, user-initiated data transfer jobs, `VpnService`, and exact alarms are in [Privacy and permissions](2-privacy-and-permissions.md#27-foreground-services).

- [ ] No interfering with, disrupting, damaging, or accessing without authorization the device, other devices, servers, networks, APIs, or services, including other apps, Google services, or a carrier network
- [ ] Follows the default Android system optimization requirements in the Core App Quality guidelines
- [ ] The app does not modify, replace, or update itself by any means other than Google Play's update mechanism. SDK self-update code counts
- [ ] No executable code (dex, JAR, `.so`) downloaded from outside Google Play, by the app or an SDK
- [ ] Code in a virtual machine or interpreter that gives only indirect access to Android APIs (such as JavaScript in a webview or browser) is exempt
- [ ] Interpreted code (JavaScript, Python, Lua) loaded at run time and not packaged with the app does not allow potential policy violations. Applies to SDKs
- [ ] No webview with an added JavaScript interface that loads untrusted web content (for example an `http://` URL) or unverified URLs from untrusted sources (for example URLs from untrusted Intents)
- [ ] No code that introduces or exploits security vulnerabilities. Check flags from the App Security Improvement Program. An SDK that downloads files over an insecure connection is an example
- [ ] No blocking or interfering with another app's ads
- [ ] No game cheating that affects other apps' gameplay
- [ ] No hacking or circumvention instructions or tools for services, software, or hardware
- [ ] No use of a service or API that breaks its terms of service
- [ ] Apps not eligible for allowlisting do not try to bypass system power management
- [ ] Proxy services for third parties only where that is the primary, user-facing core purpose of the app
- [ ] No installing other apps without the user's prior consent, and no linking to or facilitating malicious software
- [ ] No circumventing Android sandbox protections to learn user activity or identity from other apps
- [ ] No full-screen intent used to force interaction with disruptive ads or notifications

**Evidence:** search for `DexClassLoader`, `PathClassLoader`, `System.load`, `dlopen`, and `Runtime.exec` fed by downloaded files (these are detection hints, not policy text). Check `addJavascriptInterface` against the URLs loaded in that webview. Check for `REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES` and install flows, `PackageInstaller` use, and self-update logic. Flag hot-update or over-the-air code delivery for interpreted code (React Native bundles, Flutter code push) as `Verify`: it is allowed only if it cannot enable policy violations. Policy does not name these frameworks.

**Violations Google lists:** an app or SDK that downloads dex or native code from outside Google Play; a JavaScript-interface webview loading `http://` or Intent-supplied URLs; installing apps without consent; an SDK with self-update code; proxy services that are not the core purpose.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/16559646

## 3.2 AppFunctions (from 2027-04-14)

Applies to apps that expose functions through the AppFunctions API. Not a current violation before 2027-04-14. Policy Deadlines and the announcement dated 2026-10-29 carry the rule.

- [ ] The app follows all existing Google Play policies for its AppFunctions
- [ ] No deceiving or manipulating AI agents
- [ ] No bypassing security controls
- [ ] No interfering with other applications

Detail from the Preview: Permissions and APIs page: function names, parameters, and descriptions match runtime behavior; no hidden system instructions or prompts returned dynamically in runtime responses (instructions for agents are declared at registration); no dictating execution rules for other apps' AppFunctions; no coaxing agents to reveal system instructions or user data; no interfering with an agent's ability to pick or call other apps; schemas limited to what the tool needs; data collected through AppFunctions covered in Data safety and the User Data policy.

**Evidence:** AppFunctions declarations and their descriptions, and whether runtime responses carry instruction-like text aimed at an agent.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/16909972

## 3.3 Deceptive behavior

Policy has five parts: misleading claims, deceptive device settings changes, enabling dishonest behavior, manipulated media, and behavior transparency.

**Misleading claims**

- [ ] Title, icon, screenshots, description, and all other metadata describe the real functionality accurately
- [ ] No functionally impossible claims, even as a prank, fake, or joke (an insect repellent app, a phone breathalyzer)
- [ ] Rating and category are correct
- [ ] No false or deceptive content that could interfere with voting or election outcomes
- [ ] No false claim of affiliation with a government entity, or of providing government services without authorization
- [ ] No "official app" claim, or titles such as "[Celebrity] Official", without the rights

**Device settings changes**

- [ ] No change to device settings or features outside the app without the user's knowledge and consent. This covers system and browser settings, bookmarks, shortcuts, icons, widgets, and homescreen presentation
- [ ] Consented changes are easily reversible
- [ ] No settings changes as a service to third parties or for advertising
- [ ] No misleading users into removing or disabling third-party apps or changing settings or features. No encouraging or incentivizing it either, unless it is part of a verifiable security service

**Enabling dishonest behavior**

- [ ] No generators for ID cards, social security numbers, passports, diplomas, credit cards, bank accounts, or driver's licenses
- [ ] Extra resources (such as game assets) are downloaded only if necessary. Prompt the user and disclose the download size first. Applies to CDN downloads
- [ ] A "prank" or "for entertainment" label does not exempt an app
- [ ] No mimicking apps or sites to get personal or authentication information
- [ ] No unverified or real phone numbers, contacts, addresses, or personal information of non-consenting people
- [ ] Core functionality that differs by geography, device parameters, or other user data is prominently advertised in the listing
- [ ] Significant changes between versions are disclosed in what's new and in the listing

**Manipulated media**

- [ ] No promoting or creating demonstrably false or misleading imagery, audio, video, or text that may cause harm about a sensitive event, politics, social issues, or public concern
- [ ] Exceptions: public interest, clearly artificial images, media with user-facing disclaimers or watermarks, obvious satire or parody
- [ ] The listing does not use public figures or sensitive-event media to advertise media-altering features

**Behavior transparency**

- [ ] **No hidden, dormant, or undocumented features, and no review evasion.** Trace remote flags that switch behavior on after approval, and any branch on reviewer IP, emulator, or device
- [ ] No manipulating or modifying behavior during review, and no misleading reviewers about purpose or function (clarified 2026-10-29, enforcement standard unchanged)
- [ ] No mimicking OS or other app functionality or warnings

Do not flag ordinary feature flags, staged rollouts, or A/B tests unless they conceal functionality from review. Do not flag root or emulator detection without evidence of review evasion.

**Evidence:** compare the listing to the real UI; read remote config and feature flag defaults; check how geography or device checks change core features; check the manifest for settings-writing permissions such as `WRITE_SETTINGS`; confirm a size prompt before large downloads.

**Violations Google lists:** a racing game listing for a block puzzle game; an antivirus app that is only a removal guide; breathalyzer or insect-repellent apps; wrong rating or category; election falsehoods; false government affiliation; "Official" celebrity titles; apps that mimic others to steal credentials; unadvertised geography-based core differences; silent major version changes; changing behavior in review; CDN downloads with no size prompt; news-broadcast mimics with real outlet logos and no watermark.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/17006354

## 3.4 Misrepresentation, impersonation, and target API

**Misrepresentation** applies to apps and developer accounts.

- [ ] No impersonating a person or organization, and no hiding or misrepresenting ownership or primary purpose
- [ ] No coordinated activity to mislead users, including hiding or misrepresenting country of origin while directing content at users in another country
- [ ] No coordination with other apps, sites, developers, or accounts to hide developer or app identity or other material details where content relates to politics, social issues, or public concern

**Impersonation**

- [ ] The app does not imply a relationship to, or authorization by, another company, developer, entity, organization, or app that the developer does not actually have
- [ ] Icons, titles, descriptions, and in-app elements do not mislead about the app's relationship to someone else
- [ ] Developer name does not suggest a relationship to Google or another company without one
- [ ] No national emblems that suggest government ties, and no copied business or website logos
- [ ] Titles and icons are not so close to existing products that users may be misled
- [ ] No "official" claims, such as "[Celebrity] Official", without rights
- [ ] Android references follow the Android Brand Guidelines
- [ ] No pretending to be another app to trick users into actions meant for the trusted app (Social Engineering)

**Target API level** (details in [Console and release](7-console-and-release.md#73-target-api-level)): new apps and updates must target an API level within one year of the latest major Android release or submission is blocked. Unupdated apps not within two years are hidden from new users on newer Android versions.

**Violations Google lists:** a developer name implying a Google relationship; a national emblem implying government ties; a copied business logo; a cryptocurrency website's logo in the icon; a famous TV show's character and title in an icon.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9888689 and https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9888374

## 3.5 SDKs

The developer is responsible for every SDK and for third-party code behavior. SDKs must align with the app's policy-compliant use of data.

- [ ] No SDK sells personal and sensitive user data, whether sent to a server or collected by embedded code. User-initiated transfers are not sales
- [ ] SDK data access is limited to purposes users reasonably expect, handled securely (modern cryptography such as HTTPS), and gated by runtime permission requests where available
- [ ] Unexpected SDK data use meets the prominent disclosure and consent rules
- [ ] For SDKs that collect personal and sensitive data by default, evidence of prominent disclosure and consent can be produced within 2 weeks of a Google Play request, or the longer period given in the request
- [ ] Persistent device identifiers (IMEI, IMSI, SIM Serial) are not linked to other personal and sensitive data or to resettable identifiers. Exceptions: SIM-linked telephony, and enterprise device management in device owner mode, both with prominent disclosure
- [ ] Data collected through SDKs is declared in the Data safety section, and it matches the privacy policy
- [ ] Permissions and sensitive APIs used by an SDK are necessary for features promoted in the listing
- [ ] Child-directed apps include only SDKs that self-certified for child-directed use (see [Families](6-families.md#65-families-self-certified-ads-sdk-program))
- [ ] SDK foreground services have a valid use case and are declared in the app manifest
- [ ] SDKs meet Malware, Mobile Unwanted Software, Device and Network Abuse, and Deceptive Behavior rules. An SDK must not evade app review

**Evidence:** list SDKs from `build.gradle` or the dependency report, then check each for network calls, permissions, and identifiers in the merged manifest. Check the Google Play SDK Index for outdated or non-compliant versions (`Verify`: the SDK Index is not part of the policy text).

**Field report:** libraries that add permissions to the merged manifest cause rejections the developer did not expect. Example: Expo's `expo-video` merging `FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MEDIA_PLAYBACK` even with background playback disabled in config (Expo issue 39988). Inspect the merged manifest of the release build, not just the app config.

**Violations Google lists:** an SDK that collects personal data without treating it as user data; an SDK that claims anti-fraud only but shares data for ads or analytics; an SDK sending installed packages without prominent disclosure; an SDK linking IMEI with location; an SDK linking the advertising ID to persistent identifiers or email; an SDK requesting background location for an undisclosed purpose; an SDK sending IMEI from `READ_PHONE_STATE` without consent; an SDK sending audio or call recordings unrelated to function; an SDK billing users through the phone bill by trickery; an SDK that uses foreground services without a use case, or one not declared in the manifest.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/13323374

## 3.6 Malware and mobile unwanted software

Malware is any code that could put a user, their data, or a device at risk. The rules apply to third-party code, including SDKs. Code can be flagged even if harm was not intended.

**Malware categories**

- [ ] No backdoors: code allowing unwanted, remote-controlled operations. Dynamic code loading that is used to extract SMS is a backdoor. Arbitrary code execution with no sign of malicious intent is treated as a vulnerability to patch
- [ ] No billing fraud: premium SMS without consent (or hiding disclosures or carrier confirmations), premium calls without consent, or toll fraud (carrier, WAP, or airtime billing, including silent clicks on a transparent webview)
- [ ] No denial of service, such as high-volume HTTP requests to overload remote servers
- [ ] No hostile downloaders: code made to spread harmful apps, or whose downloads are at least 5% harmful with at least 500 observed downloads (25 harmful). Major browsers and file-sharing apps are exempt if all downloads are user initiated
- [ ] No phishing: code posing as a trusted source to collect credentials or billing information, or intercepting credentials in transit
- [ ] No elevated privilege abuse: breaking the sandbox, stealing OAuth tokens from other apps, preventing uninstall or stop, disabling SELinux
- [ ] No ransomware: locking the device or encrypting data for payment, or using device policy manager features to block removal. Subsidized device management code that meets lock, disclosure, and consent rules may be excluded
- [ ] No rooting without the user told in advance, and no other harmful action alongside it
- [ ] No spam: unsolicited messages to contacts, or using the device as an email spam relay
- [ ] No spyware: collecting, exfiltrating, or sharing user or device data unrelated to policy-compliant function, including recording audio or calls and stealing app data
- [ ] No trojans: harmless-looking apps with a hidden harmful part
- [ ] No riskware: obfuscation, dynamic code loading, or cloaking to show different or fake functionality
- [ ] No non-Android threats (components harmful to other platforms)

**Monitoring apps (stalkerware)**: only apps designed and marketed exclusively for parents monitoring children, or enterprises monitoring employees, are acceptable. Not for tracking a spouse, even with consent.

- [ ] The manifest uses the `IsMonitoringTool` metadata flag. Help article: the value is `child_monitoring`, `enterprise_management`, or `other` (`other` gets a case-by-case exemption review), on all version codes across all tracks
- [ ] Not presented as spying or secret surveillance, and tracking is not hidden or cloaked
- [ ] A persistent notification whenever the app runs, and a unique icon that identifies the app
- [ ] Monitoring is disclosed in the store description
- [ ] The listing does not link to a non-compliant APK hosted outside Google Play
- [ ] Prominent disclosure and consent per the User Data policy

**Mobile unwanted software (MUwS)**

- [ ] The app delivers every function it communicates, and explains system changes and lets users review and approve significant installation options
- [ ] No false claims that the device is in a critical security state or infected
- [ ] No invalid activity designed to increase ad traffic or conversions
- [ ] No requests, tricks, or rewards (extra features) to turn off device protections such as Google Play Protect
- [ ] Personal and sensitive data handled as the User Data policy requires, with secure transmission
- [ ] No ads shown in unexpected ways: impairing device functions, or displayed outside the app without being easily dismissable and with adequate consent and attribution
- [ ] No interfering with other apps or device usability, and uninstall is clear
- [ ] No mimicking OS or other apps' prompts, and no suppressing alerts from other apps or the OS, especially those about OS changes
- [ ] System notifications are used only for integral features (for example an airline's deals alert), and never to serve ads
- [ ] No ad fraud: hidden ads, automatic ad clicks, fake install attribution clicks, ads popping up outside the app, spoofing another OS or a different package name to ad networks
- [ ] Bundled software is disclosed
- [ ] No hostile downloaders of unwanted software, under the same 5% and 500 download test as above

**Evidence:** `SmsManager` or premium-number calls, hidden or zero-size webviews, root checks that run `su` commands, `DevicePolicyManager` calls that block uninstall, and ad code that triggers clicks. Verify that a monitoring app sets the flag and shows the notification.

**Violations Google lists:** an SDK from a provider that distributes malware; stealing OAuth tokens; abusing features to prevent uninstall; disabling SELinux; ads delivered through a system notification; ads that look like app UI; hidden ads; automatic ad clicks; fake install attribution; popup ads outside the app.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9888380 and https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9970222

## 3.7 FLAG_SECURE, on-device containers, and full-screen intent

- [ ] Apps do not facilitate or create workarounds that bypass another app's `FLAG_SECURE`. Accessibility Tools are exempt if they do not transmit, save, or cache protected content for access outside the device
- [ ] Apps that provide on-device Android containers read the manifests of apps they load, do not load apps that declare `REQUIRE_SECURE_ENV`, do not proxy device APIs to make them appear installed in the container, and do not work around the flag (for example by loading an older version)
- [ ] `USE_FULL_SCREEN_INTENT` (target API 34+) is granted automatically only when core function is setting an alarm or receiving phone or video calls. Otherwise the user must grant it. It must not interfere with, disrupt, or access the device in an unauthorized manner

**Evidence:** `FLAG_SECURE` handling in screen capture or accessibility code; `REQUIRE_SECURE_ENV` in the manifest of apps that opt out of containers; `USE_FULL_SCREEN_INTENT` in the merged manifest and the notification it fires.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/16559646 and https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/13609005

# 4. Monetization and Ads

Basis: Developer Program Policy effective 2026-10-29 and the linked help pages. A rule not yet in force carries `(from YYYY-MM-DD)`. Never report those as current violations.

## Contents

- 4.1 Payments (what must use Play billing, steering, AI and chat purchases)
- 4.2 Subscriptions
- 4.3 Ads
- 4.4 Regional billing programs
- 4.5 Play Billing Library versions

## 4.1 Payments

**Establish the facts before flagging.** A non-Play checkout is not automatically a violation. Find out what is sold (digital or physical), where it is sold, and whether the developer is enrolled in a regional program. If you cannot tell, report what needs verifying.

| Sold through the app | Default | Notes |
|---------------------|---------|-------|
| Paid app download | Play billing | |
| Digital goods and features: virtual currency, extra lives, add-ons, characters, ad-free upgrade, new paid features, subscriptions, cloud software and services | Play billing | Unless an enrolled regional program applies (4.4) |
| Physical goods, physical services (transport, airfare, gym membership, food delivery, live-event tickets), credit card or utility bill remittance | Play billing **must not** be used | |
| Peer-to-peer payments, online auctions, tax-exempt donations, online gambling, categories banned by the Payments Center content policy | Play billing **must not** be used | |
| Regulated clinical services (licensed provider, to diagnose or manage a medical condition) | Not Play billing | Example: doctor consult, prescription, treatment plan |
| Insurance, stock trades, investment consulting, tax preparation and filing | Not Play billing | Payments FAQ says these should not use it |
| Digital goods that can only be used outside the Play app | Play billing not required | Example: web-only content never consumed in the app |
| Gift cards sold in app | Play billing not required | |
| Earned or awarded points | Play billing not required | Selling points or virtual currency does require it |
| Tips where 100% goes to the creator and nothing digital is unlocked | Peer-to-peer, not required | If any condition fails, Play billing is required |
| 1:1 live paid service between two individuals, not recorded or replayable in a Play app | Not required | |
| Mixed digital and physical SKU | Play billing for SKUs with more digital than physical content, or marketed as digital | |
| Carrier or cable bill payment for bundled digital goods | Allowed only for eligible providers, in apps for managing the service or for subscribers | Needs Google's form |

**Fact checks.** Play billing is not required in a country where Google Play billing is not available. Tokenized assets such as NFTs bought as in-app digital content still need Play billing.

**Steering.** Outside a regional program, the app must not lead users to another payment method through any of:

- The Play listing
- In-app promotions for purchasable content
- Webviews, buttons, links, messaging, ads, or other calls to action
- UI flows, including sign-up or account creation flows

Allowed: links to administrative pages (account, privacy, help) that do not lead on to an alternate payment. Communication outside the app, such as email or special offers, is allowed. A consumption-only app (nothing can be bought in the app) may show plain text such as "go to our website" with no link.

**AI, chat agents, embedded experiences, and plugins.** If a Play-managed app facilitates purchases of digital goods, services, content, features, or functionality, the Payments policy applies in every implementation. That includes a purchase started in a chat agent, or inside a third-party embedded app experience or plugin. Check for: an assistant that takes payment or links to checkout; an embedded mini-app or plugin with its own checkout; deep links from a chat reply to a web store for digital items.

- [ ] Prices shown match the price in the Play billing screen. If the listing refers to features that cost extra, the listing says payment is required
- [ ] Virtual currency works only in the app or game title it was bought in
- [ ] Odds for randomized items (loot boxes) are disclosed before the purchase, and close to it in time and place
- [ ] The app uses a supported Play Billing Library version (see 4.5)
- [ ] Purchases are acknowledged, and verified on a server when they unlock value: `Verify` against the Play Billing docs. Not covered by the policy text read
- [ ] Enrolled in a program wherever a non-Play payment or outbound link exists (see 4.4)

**Evidence:** search the whole tree for every route to outside payment, including donation links, because each one counts and a fix that misses one fails again. Check bundled HTML and changelogs, and check that a flavor flag really hides each link on the Play build. Also check checkout code and URLs, webview targets, deep links, store-page links, SKU lists, billing client calls, listing text about paid features, and any agent or plugin that completes a purchase.

**Violations Google lists:**

- An in-app button, link, webview, or sign-up flow that leads to a non-Play payment
- Virtual currency usable in a different title
- Loot box odds missing or shown only after purchase
- In-app price different from the Play billing price

Sources: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9858738 and https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/10281818

## 4.2 Subscriptions

**When it applies:** the app sells any subscription or free trial.

- [ ] Before purchase, the screen states the offer terms, total cost, billing frequency, automatic renewal, and whether a subscription is needed to use the app. The user does not need to take any extra step to see this
- [ ] Monthly plans say they renew and charge every month
- [ ] Annual or multi-month plans do not headline the monthly equivalent as the main price. The real charge is the most prominent
- [ ] Price and terms are fully localized (language and currency)
- [ ] Promotions make clear the user can reach content without subscribing, when that is true. A clear dismiss button exists
- [ ] The purchase flow does not use several screens or repeated taps in one place that end in an accidental subscribe
- [ ] SKU and offer names are accurate. "Free Trial" is not used for an auto-recurring plan
- [ ] The subscription gives sustained or recurring value. One-time benefits (lump-sum credits or currency, single-use boosters) use in-app products. Bonuses may only add to recurring value. No cutting the benefit after the first period
- [ ] A subscription is not cancelled without the user's request after delivering a one-time benefit
- [ ] Free trial or intro offer: states duration, price after the offer, when and how it converts to paid, how to cancel, and what content is available without the trial. The post-trial charge is easy to read
- [ ] Account settings (or an equivalent page) disclose how to manage or cancel, and give an easy online route: a link to Google Play's Subscription Center, direct access to the app's own cancellation, or both
- [ ] Refund wording matches policy. By default, cancelling gives no refund for the current period, and access continues to period end. Local law can differ. Any more generous refund policy is the developer's to publish, and policy changes must be notified to users
- [ ] (from 2027-01-27) Subscriptions with ongoing eligibility requirements, such as student plans, disclose how eligibility is decided and verified, the non-discounted price or alternate plan the user moves to, and any change in benefits. Eligibility criteria must be clear and valid

**Evidence:** paywall and plan-selection screens in every locale, SKU and base-plan names, trial copy, account settings screen, and the Play Console subscription setup.

**Violations Google lists:**

- Monthly plan that does not say it renews monthly
- Annual plan most prominently showing the monthly cost
- Partly localized pricing and terms
- SKU named "Free Trial" for an auto-billing plan
- Several screens that lead to an accidental subscribe
- Benefit cut sharply after the first period (1,000 gems, then 1)
- No manage or cancel link in account settings
- Trial with unclear length, no auto-enrolment notice, or hard-to-read post-trial charge

Sources: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9900533 and the preview https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/18204939

## 4.3 Ads

**When it applies:** the app shows ads or ad-like offers. Ads and their offers count as part of the app. Flag only what code or a captured screen shows, since timing is often set at runtime.

**Content and honesty**

- [ ] Ad content and linked offers suit the app's content rating
- [ ] Ads do not mimic app features, system notifications, or warnings, and it is clear which app serves each ad
- [ ] No ads or offers delivered through system notifications or alerts. System notifications are for the app's integral features
- [ ] No forced ad click or personal data submission before full use of the app
- [ ] Fully dismissible ads: no missing dismiss button, no false dismiss button, no ad that appears where users tap for functions

**Placement and timing**

- [ ] Ads appear only inside the app serving them. None on the home screen, none triggered by home or exit, no overlay, companion, or widgetized ad units, and no interference with other apps, system or device buttons, or ports
- [ ] No unexpected full-screen interstitial, such as after a tap but before the tapped action takes effect
- [ ] No ad at the start of a game level or at the start of a content segment
- [ ] No full-screen video interstitial before the splash or loading screen
- [ ] Full-screen interstitials can be closed within 15 seconds. Opt-in interstitials, and ones that do not interrupt an action (for example after a score screen), may last longer
- [ ] Not subject to the Better Ads items above: rewarded ads the user explicitly opts into, video with integrated ads, and non-full-screen banners
- [ ] No back-to-back interstitials after consecutive user actions (the Made for Ads rule)
- [ ] No lock-screen ads or lock-screen monetization, unless the app's exclusive purpose is a lockscreen

**Fraud**

- [ ] No hidden or invisible ads, no automatic clicks, no fake install attribution clicks
- [ ] No ads popped up when the user is outside the app
- [ ] No false inventory claims, such as misreporting the platform or package name to an ad network

**Data and identifiers**

- [ ] Location used for ads is clear to the user, written in the privacy policy, and links the relevant ad network privacy policies
- [ ] Location permission is never requested solely for ads
- [ ] Advertising ID rules in 2.1 are met. For ads, the app uses the advertising ID in place of other device identifiers when it is available
- [ ] Apps that update their target to Android 13 (API 33) or higher declare `com.google.android.gms.permission.AD_ID` to read the advertising ID. Ad SDKs such as play-services-ads may add it by manifest merge, so read the merged manifest. Families policy says child-only apps should not request it at API 33+. Without an advertising ID (a deleted ID reads as zeros), a persistent identifier may be a fallback only with a privacy policy shown and lawful handling. For non-ads needs such as analytics and fraud prevention, App Set ID is the intended identifier
- [ ] Apps for children use the Families rules (see 6-families.md)

**Evidence:** ad SDK config and placement calls, interstitial trigger points, screenshots of each ad slot, the manifest, the privacy policy ad section, and the Console content rating.

**Violations Google lists:**

- A Teen-rated ad in an Everyone-rated app
- An ad styled as a feature, such as a question-mark icon that opens a landing page
- Ads that mimic system notifications
- A full-screen ad with no dismiss button, or with a false one
- An ad that appears where users tap for functions
- An ad on the home screen, or one triggered by home or exit
- A static ad at level start, or a video ad at the start of a content segment
- A gameplay interstitial not skippable within 15 seconds
- An interstitial after each of two consecutive taps ("Start app", then "Service")

Sources: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9857753 and https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/6048248 (Advertising ID). Ad fraud and system-notification rules: the Ad Fraud and Unauthorized Use or Imitation of System Functionality sections of https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/18258653

## 4.4 Regional billing programs

**When it applies:** the app has a non-Play payment, or an outbound link for digital goods, in a region where programs exist. The Payments policy allows an alternative in-app billing system, and outbound links, in eligible regions only for enrolled developers who accept the program terms.

Label: **from Google's regional program pages, read as raw text on 2026-10-31.** Fee percentages are left out on purpose, because Google's fee schedule is staggered by region and by new or existing install. Look them up when a decision needs them.

| Region | Program | Conditions to check | Dates |
|--------|---------|---------------------|-------|
| US | Alternative billing, External content links | Mobile and tablet, US users. Google says it will not require Play billing in US apps and developers may tell users about other methods. Programs still need enrollment. Alternative billing must stay in the app. Transaction reporting within 24 hours via APIs. Support, dispute, and refund routes. If Play Billing is offered, keep it reliably available. External links: US users and territories only, destination rules, registered external apps for download links, refunds unless clearly non-refundable. Both programs are opt-in | Enrolled developers report transactions and pay fees from 2026-10-01. Enrolled external-link developers have until 2027-02-01 to report successful downloads and pay the download fees. A 2026-03-04 settlement awaits a revised injunction: check the US update page live |
| EEA | Alternative billing, User choice billing, External offers, Billing choice | Business-registered developer for alternative billing and external offers. EEA users only. Required APIs and 24-hour reporting. Alternative billing and external offers: any form factor. External offers: not child-only apps, listing must not mention outside purchases, enrolled apps may use alternative billing without user choice only, not Play Billing. Billing choice (mobile and tablet) offers an in-app alternative with Play Billing beside it. User choice billing and the EEA program stay available | Billing choice and new install-based fees from 2026-06-30. External offers updated fees from 2026-06-04; link-outs to app downloads since 2025-12 |
| UK, Australia | Billing choice | Mobile and tablet. Play Billing is always offered next to alternatives. A custom choice screen only if it follows UX guidelines and is set in Console. Links to own offers only. Integrate the billing choice APIs (information screen, parental controls, 24-hour reporting) | UK from 2026-06-30. Australia from 2026-09-30 |
| Japan | Billing choice. External payments (closed to new enrolment) | External payments: business-registered, mobile and tablet, links shown beside Play Billing, own items only, not for apps aimed only at under-13s, listing must not mention outside purchases. Enrolled apps move to billing choice by 2027-03-31 to keep web links. Separate legal gate: sellers into or out of Japan must finish Japan authorization or payments are held globally | Billing choice from 2026-09-30. External payments closed to new enrolment 2026-09-30 and discontinued after 2027-03-31. Authorization due 2026-12-01 |
| India | Alternative billing alongside Play | Mobile and tablet users in India. PCI DSS certification, fraud reporting route, APIs, 24-hour reporting. May use embedded-webview payments. Play Billing stays offered beside it | API reporting available since 2023-11-14 |
| South Korea | Alternative billing alongside Play | Mobile and tablet users in Korea. APIs mandatory since 2023-08-02. PCI DSS, fraud reporting, 24-hour reporting | Fee changes and new Apps and Games programs scheduled for 2026-12-31. The billing choice page does not list Korea yet |
| Elsewhere | None found | An outbound link or alternative payment for digital goods is a violation unless a program applies | The fees page schedules Rest of World fee changes and expanded billing choice for 2027-09-30. The billing choice page lists no other market yet |

- [ ] Each non-Play checkout or outbound link maps to a program the developer has joined, for that region only
- [ ] Link-outs and alternative billing are limited to the eligible users and form factors (mobile and tablet)
- [ ] Link destinations describe where the user is going before the link-out, carry no personal data in the URL unless it is secured or encrypted, do not redirect or mislead, and offer only the developer's own items
- [ ] Reporting and information-screen API calls exist where the program requires them

**Evidence:** Console enrollment status, region gating in code, the information-screen API calls, and reporting jobs.

**Violations Google lists:** none itemised on the pages read. The general steering rule in 4.1 applies where there is no enrollment.

Dates above come from each program page and the fees page. A regional program can change with a court order or settlement, so the live page wins.

Sources: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/15582165 (US update), https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/16497028 (US alternative billing), https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/16470497 (US external links), https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/12348241 (EEA), https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14372887 (EEA external offers), https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/17161464 (billing choice), https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/16787536 (Japan external payments), https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/13306652 (India), https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/11222040 (South Korea), https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/16954621 (fees), https://support.google.com/paymentscenter/answer/17595997 (Japan verification)

## 4.5 Play Billing Library versions

**When it applies:** the app uses Play billing. Source is the Play Billing deprecation FAQ, read as raw text on 2026-10-31 (page updated 2026-10-23).

**What the deadlines mean (per that page).** Every library version has a two-year deprecation cycle. The table gives each version two dates: a "new app and update deadline" and an "extension deadline". From the first date, new apps and updates to existing apps may no longer use that version and must use a later supported one. Already-published apps keep working, and unmaintained APKs need no update. The extension deadline is the last date to keep distributing on that version, and only for a developer who requests an extension through the form on the Policy status warning page in Console. A site banner confirms it for 7: by 2026-08-31 new apps and updates must use library 8 or later.

| Version | New app and update deadline | Extension deadline |
|---------|-----------------------------|--------------------|
| 7 | 2026-08-31 (passed) | 2026-11-01 |
| 8 | 2027-08-31 | 2027-11-01 |
| 9 | 2028-08-31 | 2028-11-01 |

Versions 5 and 6 are already past both dates. The dependency shows up only in APKs that require the `com.android.vending.BILLING` permission.

- [ ] The library version is supported for the release date: library 8 or later today. Without an approved extension, an update on library 7 is out of policy now. An approved library 7 extension ends 2026-11-01
- [ ] The manifest keeps the `com.google.android.play.billingclient.version` attribute. If a deprecation warning remains after upgrading, check whether manifest merging removed it
- [ ] Extensions are requested through the form on the warning's details page under Policy status.

**Evidence:** `com.android.billingclient:billing` version in Gradle, the merged manifest, and Policy status in Console.

Source: https://developer.android.com/google/play/billing/deprecation-faq

# 5. Listing and Functionality

Find listing text in `fastlane/metadata/android/`, `app/src/*/play/`, or ask the user for it. Assets (icon, feature graphic, screenshots, video URL) usually live only in Play Console. If you cannot see an item, list it under "could not verify" rather than passing it.

Policy basis: Developer Program Policy effective 2026-10-29. Dated rules live in `deadlines.md`.

## Contents

- 5.1 Metadata
- 5.2 Store assets and text limits
- 5.3 Promotion
- 5.4 Ratings, reviews, and installs
- 5.5 Content ratings
- 5.6 Spam and minimum functionality
- 5.7 Broken functionality
- 5.8 News and magazines
- 5.9 Hostile cases

## 5.1 Metadata

- [ ] App title is 30 characters or fewer. Count every character, and check each localized title you can see
- [ ] No emojis, emoticons (kaomoji included), or repeated special characters in the title, icon, or developer name
- [ ] No ALL CAPS in those elements unless it is the brand name
- [ ] No text or image in the title, icon, or developer name that indicates store performance or ranking, price or promotion, or a relation to a Google Play program
- [ ] No misleading symbol in the icon, such as a new-message dot with no messages, or a download symbol on an app that is not about downloads
- [ ] No unattributed or anonymous testimonials in the description
- [ ] No data comparison of apps or brands, and no word blocks or vertical or horizontal word lists
- [ ] Title, description, icon, screenshots, and promotional images are accurate, descriptive, relevant, and not excessive or repetitive
- [ ] Nothing in the listing is sexually suggestive, profane, graphically violent (icons, promo images, video), or shows illicit drug use. For drugs, educational or artistic framing does not lift the general-audience rule
- [ ] App category is truthful. Choosing a category to qualify for different quality thresholds is a Metadata violation

**Evidence:** The policy applies the title (30 characters), emoji, ALL CAPS, ranking, price, and program-label bans to the title, icon, and developer name. The wider "misleading, improperly formatted, non-descriptive, irrelevant, excessive" test covers description, developer name, title, icon, screenshots, and promotional images. The category rule comes from the technical quality page FAQ.

**Violations Google lists:** unattributed or anonymous user testimonials; data comparison of apps or brands; word blocks and word lists; ALL CAPS that is not the brand name; irrelevant special character sequences; emoji, emoticon, and special-character use; misleading symbol; misleading text; images or text such as "App of the year", "#1", "Popular", award icons; "10% off", "$50 cash back"; "Editor's choice", "New"; sexually suggestive imagery; profane or vulgar language; prominent graphic violence in icons, promo images, or video; illicit drug use.

**Scope of the ranking, price, and program-label bans.** Both the Metadata and App Promotion policy text, and the Metadata help page, limit them to the app title, icon, and developer name. The asset page repeats them as a requirement for the icon (badges or text suggesting ranking, price, or Play categories), and as "highly recommended" guidance only for the short description, feature graphic, screenshots, and video. The policy's example list of violations names the items ("#1", "10% off", "Editor's choice") without naming where they appear, so it does not widen the rule. Ranking, price, or program text in a screenshot, video, feature graphic, or short description is therefore a risk under the general misleading or excessive metadata test, not a named violation. Say which sentence you relied on. The asset page allows Google Play awards such as "Best Of" in video text.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9898842

## 5.2 Store assets and text limits

Missing or malformed required assets block the listing. The asset page says failing its "Requirements" can lead to removal or suspension.

- [ ] App icon: 32-bit PNG with alpha, 512 x 512 px, at most 1024 KB, no badges or text suggesting ranking, price, Play categories, or otherwise misleading
- [ ] Short description present, at most 80 characters
- [ ] Feature graphic present: JPEG or 24-bit PNG with no alpha, 1024 x 500 px
- [ ] At least 2 screenshots across device types: JPEG or 24-bit PNG with no alpha, each side 320 to 3840 px, long side no more than twice the short side. Up to 8 per device type
- [ ] Chromebook and tablet listings: the page advises at least 4 screenshots (not under its Requirements heading), 1080 to 7680 px, 16:9 landscape or 9:16 portrait
- [ ] Wear OS: at least 1 screenshot of the current version, 1:1, at least 384 x 384 px, app UI only, no device frame, no transparency or masking
- [ ] Android TV: at least 1 TV screenshot and a banner, 1280 x 720 px, JPEG or 24-bit PNG with no alpha
- [ ] Android Automotive OS: screenshots required unless the app is in a parked category. If given, at least 2 portrait (800 x 1,280 px) and 2 landscape (1,024 x 768 px), generic system UI, not vehicle or OEM specific
- [ ] Android XR: 4 to 8 screenshots, PNG or JPEG, at most 8 MB each, 8:5 ratio
- [ ] Preview video (optional): one YouTube video URL, not a playlist or channel, no extra parameters such as timecodes. Ads off (monetization off, and no copyright monetization claims), public or unlisted (not private), not age-restricted, embeddable

**Evidence:** Specs are from the Play asset page. Items under its "Highly recommended" heading are eligibility guidance and do not affect the listing page: at least 4 screenshots at 1080 px or more for apps (at least 3 for games) to be eligible for screenshot-based recommendations; taglines under 20% of the image; no calls to action; no fake or empty status bar; no other store badge; no third-party trademarked characters or logos without permission; device imagery discouraged. Report these as advisory.

Text limits (app name 30, short description 80, full description 4,000 characters) are from https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9859152. Repetitive or irrelevant keywords in any of them can lead to suspension.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9866151

## 5.3 Promotion

- [ ] No deceptive ads on websites, apps, or other properties, including notifications that resemble system notifications or alerts
- [ ] No sexually explicit ads that send users to the Play listing
- [ ] No promotion or install tactics that redirect users to Google Play or download apps without informed user action
- [ ] No unsolicited promotion by SMS
- [ ] The developer answers for its ad networks, affiliates, and ads

**Evidence:** The App Promotion policy bans apps that directly or indirectly engage in, or benefit from, promotion that is deceptive or harmful.

**Violations Google lists:** the first four bullets above, plus the ranking, price, and program-text bullet in 5.1.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9899004

## 5.4 Ratings, reviews, and installs

- [ ] No incentive offered for a rating (for example a discount for a high rating)
- [ ] No fake, repeated, or purchased ratings, reviews, or installs, and no posing as users to influence placement
- [ ] No encouraging reviews that contain affiliates, coupons, game codes, email addresses, or links to sites or other apps
- [ ] The app's main function is not paying users to install other apps
- [ ] Developer replies stay on the issue raised and do not ask for a higher rating

**Evidence:** The policy forbids manipulating placement through ratings, reviews, or install counts by illegitimate means. The reply guidance is listed as a best practice, not as a named violation.

**Verify:** whether a prompt that sends only happy users to the Play listing ("review gating") is penalized. The policy text read lists incentives and fraud, not routing. Use of the In-App Review API is not stated either. Report such a flow as `Verify`.

**Violations Google lists:** rating requests with an incentive; repeatedly submitting ratings as users; reviews containing affiliates, coupons, game codes, emails, or links.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9898684

## 5.5 Content ratings

- [ ] A content rating exists for the app. Apps without one are not allowed and are removed
- [ ] The questionnaire answers match the real content. Misrepresentation can lead to removal or suspension
- [ ] The questionnaire was redone after changes to content or features that affect the answers
- [ ] Ads shown are not significantly more mature than the app's own content
- [ ] A rating dispute goes to the IARC authority through the link in the certificate email, not through a Play appeal

**Evidence:** IARC assigns the rating from the Console questionnaire. The rating covers in-app content, not ads, agreements, or age-specific privacy practices. The 2026-07-15 announcement clarified that unrated apps are not allowed.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9898843

## 5.6 Spam and minimum functionality

- [ ] Not a webview of a website, or an affiliate-traffic app, unless the site owner or administrator gave permission. Earning sign-up or purchase credit on another site as the primary purpose is the violation
- [ ] Not a copy of other apps' content without original value, and not a set of highly similar small apps that should be one app
- [ ] No SMS, email, or other messages sent for the user without letting them confirm content and recipients
- [ ] Has app-specific functionality. Static text-only or PDF apps, very thin single-wallpaper apps, and apps that do nothing are limited-functionality violations

**Evidence:** Spam, Functionality, and User Experience policy.

**Violations Google lists:** share button that sends messages unconfirmed; app whose primary purpose is a webview of a site without permission; copying content without added value; multiple highly similar apps; static text or PDF apps; single-wallpaper apps; apps designed to do nothing.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9899034

## 5.7 Broken functionality

- [ ] The app installs, loads, and responds. No crashes, force closes, freezes, or abnormal behavior on the screens a reviewer reaches first
- [ ] Pre-launch report, if available, has no Errors (crashes, ANRs, defective libraries, restricted unsupported API use)
- [ ] Sign-in, onboarding, and permission-denied paths do not dead-end

**Evidence:** The policy lists apps that do not install, install but do not load, and load but are not responsive. The pre-launch page does not say its issues block publishing. Its errors cover crashes, ANRs, defective libraries, and restricted unsupported APIs. Warnings cover slow startup, sign-in or crawl problems, memory issues, and not-yet-restricted unsupported APIs. Crashes found in the report come from test devices and do not change your crash statistics, and Google says the report cannot catch every issue. The publishing block is the release "Errors summary" in 7.1. Dead-end states are advisory, not named policy.

**Violations Google lists:** apps that do not install; apps that install but do not load; apps that load but are not responsive.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9898783 and https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9844487

## 5.8 News and magazines

- [ ] The app declares itself as News or Magazine in Play Console, with the self-declaration completed. An app also counts if it sits in the News and Magazine category and calls itself news or magazine in title, icon, developer name, or description
- [ ] Each article names its original publisher or author
- [ ] Content is updated regularly, not static
- [ ] Current contact information is clear and easy to reach
- [ ] Aggregators say who published third-party content
- [ ] A membership or subscription app shows an in-app preview before purchase
- [ ] Affiliate marketing or ad revenue is not the primary purpose

**Evidence:** News and Magazines section of the policy.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9935326

## 5.9 Hostile cases

- [ ] A localized listing, translated title, or video you cannot see: list as could not verify, not as passing
- [ ] "Free", "New", "Best", or "Sale" in the short description or screenshots: the asset page lists these as advisory for those assets. Policy-level violation only in title, icon, developer name. Report as a risk, not a named violation (see 5.1)
- [ ] YouTube video is private, age-restricted, monetized, or hits a copyright claim that adds ads: the video can fail to show
- [ ] Screenshot shows another store's badge, a fake notification bar, or third-party characters: advisory on the asset page, and a trademark problem can also be an Intellectual Property issue
- [ ] Feature graphic or screenshot exported with an alpha channel: fails the no-alpha requirement
- [ ] Thin webview wrapper of the developer's own site: the owner-permission test is met, but limited functionality (5.6) still applies
- [ ] App behaves differently by geography or device and the listing does not say so, or changes significantly between versions without a What's new note and listing update: Deceptive Behavior examples
- [ ] Code or flags that change app behavior when a reviewer runs it: the policy lists apps that modify or obfuscate behavior during review, and forbids manipulating Play review. Treat as high severity
- [ ] App claims a function a phone cannot do, or calls itself a prank or "for entertainment": the policy does not exempt it
- [ ] Rating prompt that filters users: `Verify` (5.4)

**Evidence:** Deceptive Behavior policy, with the 2026-10-29 clarification about manipulating the review process.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/17006354

# 6. Families

Load this file when any selected target age group includes children, **or** the listing, art, or wording appeals to children. Google can treat an app as child-directed from its imagery and terminology, whatever the Console says. "Works great for kids" in a listing is enough to raise this. "Children" can mean different things by locale, so legal counsel decides which age limits apply. Items marked `Verify` were not confirmed against a Google page.

Failing these requirements can lead to app removal or suspension.

## Contents

- 6.1 Target audience and Console answers
- 6.2 Requirements
- 6.3 Ads and monetization in child-directed apps
- 6.4 Social apps and features
- 6.5 Families Self-Certified Ads SDK program

## 6.1 Target audience and Console answers

- [ ] Target age groups in Play Console match the app
- [ ] More than one age group is chosen only if the app is designed for and appropriate for all of them. Apps for babies, toddlers, and preschool select only "Ages 5 & Under"
- [ ] Age groups that include both adults and children are chosen only if the app is truly designed for all ages
- [ ] Target Audience and Content, Data safety, and IARC content rating answers are accurate and agree, and are updated when the app changes
- [ ] Imagery and terminology are consistent with the declared audience. Google can override the declared audience after its own review
- [ ] Changes in the Target Audience section may be reviewed before an app update, and an app update is needed before the store reflects them. Google strongly recommends telling users through What's New or in-app notices when the target age group, ads, or in-app purchases change
- [ ] Misrepresentation in Play Console can lead to removal or suspension

**Evidence:** the Target Audience answers, store art and wording (young characters, cartoon style, "for kids"), and the Data safety answers. Per the Console help article: an app not primarily designed for children under 13 whose listing marketing suggests otherwise (youthful animation, young characters in graphic assets) may be rejected. The options are to remove those marketing elements, or to change the target age groups to children under 13 only, which requires meeting the Families policy.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9893335 and https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9867159

## 6.2 Requirements

- [ ] Content that children can reach is appropriate for children. Content that suits only some regions may be limited to those regions
- [ ] The app is not just a webview of a website, and does not have a primary purpose of driving affiliate traffic to a site without the owner's permission
- [ ] The app collects no personal and sensitive information from children without disclosure, including through APIs and SDKs. Sensitive includes authentication information, microphone and camera data, device data, Android ID, and ad usage data
- [ ] Device phone number is not requested from `TelephonyManager`
- [ ] Bluetooth uses Companion Device Manager unless the app targets only OS versions that do not support it
- [ ] Legal compliance with COPPA, GDPR, and other applicable law, including APIs and SDKs
- [ ] AR content shows a safety warning immediately upon launch of the AR section. It stresses parental supervision and reminds users to watch their physical surroundings. The app does not require a device advised against for children (policy names Daydream and Oculus)
- [ ] Social apps whose main focus is chatting with strangers or anonymous chat (chat roulette, dating, kids-focused open chat rooms, anonymous apps, "blindfold" apps) do not target children (since 2026-08-26)

**Apps that target only children:**

- [ ] Do not transmit the Android advertising ID, SIM Serial, Build Serial, BSSID, MAC, SSID, IMEI, or IMSI
- [ ] Do not request `AD_ID` when targeting API 33 or higher
- [ ] Do not request location permission or collect, use, or transmit precise location
- [ ] Contain only APIs and SDKs approved for use in primarily child-directed services. Example: an OAuth API service whose terms say it is not approved for child-directed services

**Apps that target children and older audiences:**

- [ ] Do not transmit those identifiers from children or users of unknown age
- [ ] Use non-approved APIs and SDKs only behind a neutral age screen or in a way that collects no data from children, and never require them to reach app content
- [ ] The neutral age screen asks for a free-entry birth date. Per the Console help article, presetting the birth date to the required age (for example 13) or indicating that an age is required is a flawed setup

**Evidence:** merged manifest (`AD_ID`, location, phone state), network calls to ad or analytics SDKs, `TelephonyManager` calls, the age-screen UI, SDK list, and the store listing.

**Violations Google lists:** a store listing that promotes play for children but has adult-only content; APIs whose terms forbid child-directed use; glamorizing alcohol, tobacco, or controlled substances; real or simulated gambling; violence, gore, or shocking content; dating services or sexual or marital advice; links to websites that break Play policy; mature ads shown to children.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9893335

## 6.3 Ads and monetization in child-directed apps

Applies to all monetization: ads, cross-promotion of own and third-party apps, in-app purchase offers, and paid product placement. It applies when ads reach children or users of unknown age. Google may reject, remove, or suspend apps for overly aggressive commercial tactics.

- [ ] Only Google Play Families Self-Certified Ads SDKs show ads to those users
- [ ] Apps with mixed audiences use a neutral age screen so children get ads only from self-certified SDK versions
- [ ] No interest-based advertising or remarketing
- [ ] Ad content suits children, and ads follow the Families ad format rules
- [ ] Advertising laws and industry standards for children are met
- [ ] No ads that cover the whole screen or interfere with use without a clear way to dismiss (ad walls)
- [ ] Rewarded or opt-in ads that interfere with use can be closed after 5 seconds. Ads that do not interfere, such as video with integrated ads, may last longer
- [ ] No interstitial immediately upon app launch
- [ ] One ad placement per page: no banner with multiple offers, and no more than one banner or video ad
- [ ] Ads and promotions are clearly distinguishable from app content (no offerwalls or immersive ads that children cannot identify as ads). This includes promos for the developer's other listings
- [ ] No shocking or emotionally manipulative tactics to push ad views or purchases
- [ ] No dismiss button that triggers another ad, and no ads that suddenly appear where users usually tap
- [ ] Virtual game coins are clearly distinguished from real money in purchases
- [ ] No ads that move away from a finger
- [ ] No ads for: age-inappropriate media (TV, film, music), age-inappropriate games or software, alcohol, tobacco, or controlled substances, simulated gambling, contests or sweepstakes (even free), sexually suggestive content, dating or relationship sites, or violent and graphic content

Exceptions from the self-certified SDK rule, per the SDK program page: in-house advertising where SDKs manage cross-promotion of your own apps or owned media, and direct deals with advertisers where an SDK only manages inventory. Ad content and data collection must still meet the User Data and Families policies.

**Evidence:** ad SDK list and its child-directed settings flags, the ad placements in layouts, and the neutral age screen path.

**Violations Google lists:** ads that move away from a finger; no exit after 5 seconds; ads covering most of the screen with no clear close; banners with multiple offers; ads mistaken for app content; own-listing promos indistinguishable from app content.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9893335 and https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9900633

## 6.4 Social apps and features

Applies when children are in the target audience.

- [ ] Social apps (main focus is sharing freeform content or communicating with large groups) show an in-app reminder to stay safe online and about real-world risk before child users exchange freeform media or information, and require adult action before child users exchange personal information
- [ ] Social features (extra functionality that lets users share freeform content or talk to large groups) give the same reminder and let adults manage them for child users (turn on or off, set levels), and require adult action before enabling personal-information exchange
- [ ] Adult action is a mechanism that verifies the user is not a child and does not encourage children to falsify their age. Examples: adult PIN, password, birthdate, email verification, photo ID, credit card, SSN
- [ ] Sharing or exchange features are disclosed in the content rating questionnaire

**Evidence:** the screen shown before chat or sharing, the parent gate, and the content rating answers.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9893335

## 6.5 Families Self-Certified Ads SDK program

Applies to ads SDKs and mediation platforms in apps in the Families program. For the app auditor, the practical test is the list below. Google says new applicants may join (2026-10-29).

- [ ] Each ads SDK in a child-directed app is a self-certified version listed in the Help Center or SDK Index
- [ ] The SDK is set for child-directed treatment, which disables personalized ads, interest-based ads, and remarketing, on a per-request or per-app basis
- [ ] Mediation uses only certified SDKs, or has safeguards that make mediated ads meet the rules, and passes ad content rating and child-directed treatment information
- [ ] The SDK does not transmit the advertising ID, SIM Serial, Build Serial, BSSID, MAC, SSID, IMEI, or IMSI from children or users of unknown age

SDK provider duties (not checked in the app): ratings of ad creatives with at least Everyone and Mature groups; real-time bidding creatives reviewed and privacy indicators passed to bidders; a visual mark on creatives from its inventory; ad formats that follow the Families rules; an English terms of service, privacy policy, and integration guide; a sample test app APK; compliance with COPPA and GDPR.

**Evidence:** every ads SDK and mediation adapter in the dependency report, plus their version numbers against the certified list.

Source: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/12918983
